unit.title: Gear and Paddle Science
unit.summary: Paddle materials, construction, surface roughness, the spin-rate test, balls, shoes and the gear that changes the game.

lessons.title: What paddles are made of
lessons.objective: Contrast fiberglass, carbon, composite; core types.

payload.prompt: Match each paddle face material to its feel.

pairs.definition: A softer face material that gives more pop and comfort on contact.
A stiffer face that usually gives more spin and a crisper, more responsive feel.
A blend of materials that tries to balance pop, spin, and durability.

distractorDefinitions: The core layer in the center

explanation.summary: Paddle faces come in three main types: fiberglass (soft), carbon (spinny), and composite (balanced).
explanation.sayThisLine: Fiberglass is softer, carbon is spinnier, composite balances them.

payload.prompt: Which paddle face material gives the most spin?

image.alt: Three paddle faces: fiberglass (smooth), carbon (textured gritty surface), composite (medium texture)

options.text: Fiberglass (smooth face)
Carbon (textured, gritty face)
Composite (medium texture)

explanation.correct: Raw carbon faces are usually the grittiest, and a gritty face grips the ball more, creating spin.
explanation.incorrect: It is the surface texture that grips the ball, and raw carbon faces are usually the grittiest. Fiberglass and composite are typically smoother, though finishes vary by brand.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rough face = more spin. That's the carbon edge.

payload.prompt: What is a paddle core and why does it matter?

options.text: The center layer that affects feel, sound and responsiveness.
The outer edge of the paddle.
A type of face material.
The grip handle part.

explanation.correct: The core is sandwiched between the face layers; it changes how the paddle sounds and plays.
explanation.incorrect: The core is the middle layer. It affects the paddle's feel, dampening (quiet vs loud) and power.
explanation.sayThisLine: Core matters: polymer is softer and quieter, Nomex is firmer and louder.

payload.prompt: Polymer cores tend to feel softer and sound quieter than Nomex. True?

scene.alt: Paddle core material and sound relationship.

explanation.correct: Yes. Polymer honeycomb cores are softer and quieter, which is why they are the standard today. Nomex is firmer and pops louder.
explanation.incorrect: Polymer is the quieter, softer core. Nomex is firmer with a louder pop, which is one reason some courts and neighbors prefer polymer.
explanation.sayThisLine: Polymer is the quiet one. Nomex is the loud, firm one.

payload.prompt: Complete the paddle anatomy statement.
payload.template: A paddle's {{face}} affects spin, while the {{core}} affects feel.

explanation.correct: Face material controls spin; core controls sound and responsiveness.
explanation.incorrect: Face (fiberglass vs carbon) makes the spin difference. Core (polymer vs Nomex) makes the feel and sound difference.
explanation.sayThisLine: Face = spin. Core = feel. Both matter.

lessons.title: Shape and swing weight
lessons.objective: Understand elongated vs standard, weight and balance.

payload.prompt: What is the main difference between a standard paddle and an elongated paddle?

options.text: Elongated paddles are longer and narrower; standard paddles are shorter and wider.
Elongated paddles are always heavier.
Elongated paddles are only for beginners.
Standard paddles have a softer core.

explanation.correct: Shape is about the proportions. Elongated adds reach but a slightly smaller sweet spot; standard is wider and more forgiving.
explanation.incorrect: Shape describes proportions: elongated is longer and narrower, standard is shorter and wider. Weight and core are separate choices.
explanation.sayThisLine: Elongated = reach. Standard = control.

payload.prompt: Longest a legal paddle's length plus width can be, in inches?

explanation.correct: Length plus width can total 24 inches, and the length can be at most 17. That cap is why elongated paddles have to be narrower.
explanation.incorrect: The cap is 24 inches for length plus width combined, with a 17-inch maximum length. Stretch one dimension and the other has to shrink.
explanation.sayThisLine: Elongated paddles are longer, so they have to be narrower to stay legal.

payload.prompt: Your friend keeps getting stretched on wide balls. Elongated or standard paddle?

situation.narrative: Your friend gets pulled wide and wants a bit more reach.

facts.label: Trade-off
facts.value: Reach vs a bigger sweet spot

options.label: Elongated: reach is the priority
options.consequence: Good fit. A longer face gets to wide balls sooner, at the cost of a slightly smaller sweet spot.
considerations: Reach helps on wide and defensive shots
Expect a slightly smaller sweet spot

options.label: Standard: a bigger sweet spot is safer
options.consequence: Standard is more forgiving, but it does not add reach. Fine if forgiveness matters more to your friend.
considerations: Standard is easier to hit cleanly
But reach is the stated goal

payload.expertNote: Elongated trades a little sweet spot for reach. It is a rule of thumb, so a demo swing beats any chart.

payload.prompt: Match each paddle property to its effect on play.

pairs.definition: A longer, narrower paddle that gives more reach but slightly less control.
A more square paddle that offers better control and a larger sweet spot.
A paddle that feels lighter during the swing, ideal for quick reactions.

explanation.summary: Shape (elongated vs standard) and swing weight (light vs heavy) both influence how the paddle plays.
explanation.sayThisLine: Shape is proportions; swing weight is how heavy it feels in your hand.

payload.prompt: Does a higher swing weight mean the paddle is heavier overall?

explanation.correct: Swing weight is how heavy the paddle feels during the swing (it depends on the balance point), not the number on the scale.
explanation.incorrect: A light paddle can have high swing weight if the weight is distributed toward the head. Swing weight is about feel, not total pounds.
explanation.sayThisLine: Swing weight = feel during the swing, not the scale weight.

lessons.title: Fit the player
lessons.objective: Match a paddle style to a described player.

payload.prompt: She says: 'I love hitting drives and putting pace on the ball.' Which paddle profile fits?

situation.narrative: You're helping someone choose a paddle based on their playstyle.

options.label: Heavier, higher swing weight, elongated
options.consequence: Correct. Power players benefit from higher swing weight and reach.
considerations: Higher swing weight = more stable on attacks

options.label: Lighter, lower swing weight, standard
options.consequence: This is a control-focused setup, not ideal for an aggressive, power-oriented player.
considerations: But this player wants power and reach

payload.expertNote: Match playstyle to paddle: control players lean light and standard; power players lean heavier and elongated. These are rules of thumb, and a heavy paddle can tire the arm, so demo before buying.

payload.prompt: She says: 'I live at the kitchen line, dinking and blocking.' Which paddle profile fits?

situation.narrative: A net player is choosing their next paddle.

options.label: Light, low swing weight, standard
options.consequence: Correct. Net players need light, responsive paddles for quick hands.

options.label: Heavy, high swing weight, elongated
options.consequence: This is built for baseline power, not net play. The net player needs speed, not mass.

payload.expertNote: Soft-game players choose light paddles with low swing weight for quick, responsive hands at the net.

payload.prompt: What is the most important first step in choosing a paddle?

options.text: Know your playstyle (power vs control) and match the paddle to it.
Buy the most expensive paddle.
Copy what the pro players use.
Get whatever is in stock.

explanation.correct: The best paddle is one that matches how you play. Your style guides the choice.
explanation.incorrect: Paddle fit starts with understanding your game. Then you find a paddle that supports it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pick a paddle that matches your game, not the brand or the price tag.

payload.prompt: Complete the paddle-fit statement.

explanation.correct: Net/control players choose light and responsive. Power players choose heavier paddles.
explanation.incorrect: Match paddle to playstyle: net play needs light and quick; baseline needs weight.
explanation.sayThisLine: Light for the net. Heavy for the baseline.

lessons.title: Approved paddles and the spin test
lessons.objective: Explain approval, roughness limits and the spin-rate test.

payload.prompt: Why do paddles need to be approved by USA Pickleball?

options.text: To ensure paddles meet size, materials and performance standards for fair play.
To promote certain brands over others.
To make the sport more expensive.
To stop paddles from being sold in stores.

explanation.correct: Approval keeps the field level. Approved paddles have passed the same checks on size, materials and surface.
explanation.incorrect: The USA Pickleball approved list is about fairness and sport integrity, not brand promotion.
explanation.sayThisLine: Approved paddles meet standards that keep the game fair.

payload.prompt: Being on the approved list means a paddle suits your game. True?

choices.label: Yes, approved means a good fit

explanation.correct: Right. Approval says the paddle meets the rules, including surface limits. Whether it suits your swing is a separate question.
explanation.incorrect: Approval only tells you the paddle is legal for sanctioned play. Fit comes from shape, weight, balance and feel, and that is what you test by demoing.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's approved, so it's legal. Whether it's right for me, I still have to demo.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I just heard about a new spin-rate test starting October 2026. I'm worried my paddle might not pass.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: It's designed to limit equipment arms races and keep the game fair.
Just buy a new paddle, everyone will.
The test is pointless, ignore it.
Only professional paddles need approval.

payload.translation: The spin-rate test (starting Oct 1, 2026) limits surface roughness to keep paddles from becoming too spinny.

followUps.line: The test measures how much spin different paddle surfaces can generate and sets a limit.
followUps.why: Explains what the test does without guessing details.

followUps.line: If your paddle isn't approved after the test, you'd need to swap, but plenty of paddles will still be legal.
followUps.why: Shows the practical outcome without being alarmist.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The spin-rate test is about keeping equipment from dominating strategy.

payload.prompt: Match each gear concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A paddle that meets USA Pickleball standards for size, materials and performance.
The texture of the paddle face; rougher surfaces create more spin.
New USA Pickleball testing (effective Oct 1, 2026) that limits paddle surface roughness.

explanation.summary: Approved paddles meet standards. The new spin-rate test limits roughness to keep equipment fair.
explanation.sayThisLine: Approved = fair. Spin test = limiting roughness for fairness.

payload.prompt: Complete the paddle approval statement.
payload.template: To play in a tournament, your paddle must be {{status}}, and the new {{test}} limits {{limit}}.

explanation.correct: Approved paddles are tournament-legal. The spin test limits roughness starting Oct 1, 2026.
explanation.incorrect: Tournament paddles must be approved. The spin-rate test controls surface roughness.
explanation.sayThisLine: Approved paddle = legal. Spin test = roughness limit.

lessons.title: Balls, indoor and outdoor
lessons.objective: Tell them apart and why they play differently.

payload.prompt: Which ball is designed for outdoor play?

image.alt: Two pickleball balls side-by-side: indoor ball with fewer, larger holes; outdoor ball with more, smaller holes

options.text: Indoor ball (fewer, larger holes)
Outdoor ball (more, smaller holes)
They are the same

explanation.correct: Outdoor balls have smaller, more numerous holes to reduce air drag in wind.
explanation.incorrect: Outdoor balls are designed to handle wind and play slightly faster. Indoor balls are softer.
explanation.sayThisLine: Outdoor = more holes, faster flight. Indoor = fewer holes, softer.

payload.prompt: Why do outdoor balls and indoor balls play differently?

options.text: Outdoor balls are harder with more holes; indoor balls are softer with fewer holes.
Indoor balls are heavier.
Outdoor balls are bigger.
There is no difference; they're the same.

explanation.correct: The hole count and hardness are key differences. Indoor balls are softer for quieter play; outdoor balls are firmer for wind resistance.
explanation.incorrect: The design is different. Indoor: softer, fewer holes. Outdoor: firmer, more holes to handle wind.
explanation.sayThisLine: Indoor is softer and quieter. Outdoor is firmer for the wind.

payload.prompt: Which ball sound is the indoor ball?

audio.description: Two pickleball impacts: a softer, duller pop from an indoor ball and a crisper, louder pop from an outdoor ball.

options.text: The softer, duller pop
The louder, crisper pop
They sound the same

explanation.correct: Indoor balls are softer, so they produce a quieter, duller sound. Outdoor balls are firmer, louder.
explanation.incorrect: Indoor balls sound softer because they are made softer. Outdoor balls sound crisper and louder.
explanation.sayThisLine: Indoor pop = softer, quieter. Outdoor pop = louder, crisper.

payload.prompt: Do balls used in tournaments have to be USA Pickleball approved?

explanation.correct: Yes. Tournament balls must be approved to ensure a level playing field.
explanation.incorrect: Sanctioned play requires approved balls. They meet weight, size and bounce standards.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tournament balls must be approved, just like paddles.

payload.prompt: Complete the ball comparison.
payload.template: Indoor balls are {{softness}} and {{sound}}, while outdoor balls are {{outdoorsoftness}} and {{outdoorsound}}.

explanation.correct: Indoor: soft, quiet. Outdoor: hard, loud. The design matches the playing environment.
explanation.incorrect: Indoor balls are softer and quieter. Outdoor balls are harder and louder because of wind resistance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Indoor = soft and quiet. Outdoor = hard and loud.

payload.prompt: Why are court shoes better than regular sneakers for pickleball?

options.text: Court shoes provide lateral support to prevent ankle and knee injuries during cutting and sliding.
They make you play faster.
Regular sneakers work fine; it doesn't matter.
Court shoes are just a fashion choice.

explanation.correct: Court shoes are built for the lateral movement that pickleball demands. They protect your feet.
explanation.incorrect: The support in court shoes is designed for side-to-side movement, which prevents injuries.
explanation.sayThisLine: Court shoes prevent ankle and knee injuries. They're an investment in your body.

payload.prompt: Tournament tomorrow but no court shoes. Play in sneakers or skip?

situation.narrative: A tournament is tomorrow and footwear is the issue.

options.label: Buy court shoes or borrow them if possible
options.consequence: Best option. The injury risk in regular sneakers isn't worth the tournament.
considerations: Court shoes are worth the investment

options.label: Play in regular sneakers
options.consequence: If you must play, take it slow and focus on safety. Court shoes next time.

payload.expertNote: Court shoes are a safety investment, not a luxury. If you can't get them, weigh the injury risk.

payload.prompt: Match each gear item to its purpose.

pairs.definition: Specialized footwear with lateral support to prevent injuries during side-to-side movement.
Protects eyes from sun glare and flying balls, especially important on outdoor courts.
Replaceable tape or wrap that keeps your hand dry and the paddle from slipping.

explanation.summary: Court shoes, eyewear and grips are gear that supports safety, comfort and performance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Shoes = safety. Grips = control. Eyewear = protection.

payload.prompt: A paddle grip becomes worn or slippery during play. Should you replace it?

choices.label: Yes, a fresh grip helps control

explanation.correct: Yes. A worn grip reduces control and increases the risk of the paddle slipping out of your hand.
explanation.incorrect: A fresh grip is part of maintenance. Control depends on having a grip that doesn't slip.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fresh grip = better control and confidence.

payload.prompt: Complete the essential gear statement.
payload.template: Court shoes prevent {{protection}}, {{grip}} keeps your paddle secure, and {{eyewear}} shields your eyes.

explanation.correct: Court shoes for safety, grips for control, eyewear for protection. All part of playing smart.
explanation.incorrect: Essential gear: court shoes (safety), fresh grips (control), eyewear (eye protection).
explanation.sayThisLine: Shoes, grips, eyewear—invest in the gear that keeps you safe and playing well.
